title: Best Smartwatches 2026: 18 Compared, £14.99 to £244 | Megastore76
metaDescription: "Smartwatch" means two different things. Under £35 you are buying a fitness tracker with a watch face; over £50 a small computer. Eighteen compared, with honest notes on blood-pressure claims and duplicate listings.
h1: Most £20 "smartwatches" are fitness trackers wearing a watch face
intro: That is not a criticism — it is the single most useful thing to know before you buy one. Below about £35 you are buying a step counter, a heart-rate sensor and a screen that shows notifications. Above about £50 you are buying a small computer with an app store, its own processor and a battery that lasts a day or two instead of a week. Both are good purchases. They are just not the same purchase, and the listings rarely make the difference clear. Eighteen watches below, from £14.99 to £244, with the honest catch on each.
updated: Every price on this page was checked against the Megastore76 store on 29 September 2026.

verdict.heading: Three answers, because there are three different buyers here
verdict.intro: If you want steps, sleep and notifications for as little money as possible, the answer is £19.99 and you can stop reading. If you want a real smartwatch — apps, payments, a proper screen — that starts around £60 and the right one depends on which phone is in your pocket. If you want something that looks like a watch and does not need charging every night, that is a different product again.

picks.label: The £19.99 answer
picks.name: ZL02 Smart Watch
picks.why: Heart rate, sleep tracking, and a listing picture that prints the price the store charges — £19.99 — with no invented rating, award or review count on it — which, as you will see further down this page, is rarer in this department than it should be. It is not a smartwatch in the app-store sense: there is no app store, no contactless payment and no third-party apps. What it does is track steps, sleep and heart rate, show you notifications, and last about a week between charges. For most people searching for a cheap smartwatch, that is exactly what they meant.

picks.why: This is where "smartwatch" starts meaning the thing you actually imagined: Samsung's own operating system, an app store, contactless payments, proper sleep and body-composition tracking, and a screen you would describe as good rather than adequate. The trade is battery — expect roughly a day or two, not a week. If your phone is an iPhone, take the Apple Watch SE at £64.95 in the table below instead; the two are the same money and each works properly only with its own phone brand.

picks.name: CZ Smart PQ2 Hybrid, Citizen
picks.why: A hybrid does the opposite trade to everything else on this page. It looks like a normal watch, it has real hands, it needs charging about once a fortnight rather than once a day, and it tracks heart rate and activity quietly underneath. What it does not have is a big bright screen for reading messages on, because it does not have a screen at all. Buy it if you want the tracking without the glowing rectangle on your wrist.

guide.heading: Five things that decide whether you will be happy with it
guide.intro: Two of these will save you money on this page specifically. The rest are what people get wrong about smartwatches generally.

points.h: Check whether a cheaper row is the same watch
points.p: The £24.99 Fitness Tracker row and the £14.99 Answer/Make Call row are, by the store's own description, substantially the same watch — the £24.99 listing says so in its own text. The same pattern repeats across this catalogue: near-identical products listed several times at different prices. Before you buy, scan the table for a cheaper row with the same specification. On this page alone that is a £10 saving for reading one line.

points.h: Blood pressure on a cheap watch is an estimate
points.p: Several watches here advertise blood-pressure monitoring. None of them is a medical device, and none should be used to make a decision about your health. Optical sensors on a wrist at this price produce a rough number that moves with how tightly the strap is done up. If you need blood-pressure readings for a medical reason, use a proper cuff. Heart rate and step counting on these watches are reasonable; blood pressure is the one to treat as a curiosity.

points.h: Your phone decides your watch, not the other way round
points.p: The Apple Watch works properly only with an iPhone. The Samsung and Google watches work properly only with Android. The budget trackers and the Citizen hybrid pair with either. If you own an iPhone and buy the Galaxy Watch 6, you have bought the wrong watch at the right price — this is the single most common expensive mistake in this category.

points.h: Battery life is the real difference, not features
points.p: A £20 tracker runs about a week. A £60 smartwatch runs about a day or two. The hybrid runs about two weeks. That is not a specification quirk — it is the central trade. A watch with an app store has a processor and a bright screen, and both eat battery. Decide which you would rather have before you compare anything else, because no product gives you both.

points.h: Ask what it actually does with no phone nearby
points.p: "Bluetooth calling" means the call goes through your phone — the watch is a speaker and a microphone, and if the phone is in another room it will not work. Only the LTE models, like the Galaxy Watch 6 LTE at £54.95, work with your phone left at home, and that needs a separate data plan from your network. If you wanted a watch to leave the phone behind, check the LTE part of the name before you buy.

faq.q: What is the difference between a cheap smartwatch and an expensive one?
faq.a: Below about £35 you are buying a fitness tracker with a watch face: steps, sleep, heart rate and notifications, with roughly a week of battery and no app store. Above about £50 you are buying a small computer — its own operating system, an app store, contactless payments — with a battery that lasts a day or two. Both are legitimate; they are just different products, and the listings rarely say which one they are selling.

faq.q: Why is one watch listed at two different prices?
faq.a: We do not know why, and the store's own description for the £24.99 listing says it is the same watch as a lower-priced one. Near-identical products appear at several prices across this catalogue. The practical answer: check the table for a cheaper row with the same specification before you buy — on this page that is a £10 saving for one line of reading.

faq.q: Can a cheap smartwatch really measure blood pressure?
faq.a: Not in any way you should rely on. Several watches here list blood-pressure monitoring, and none is a medical device. Wrist sensors at this price produce an estimate that shifts with strap tightness and movement. Heart rate and step counting on these watches are reasonable; treat blood pressure as a curiosity, and use a proper cuff if you need the number for a medical reason.

faq.q: Will a Samsung or Apple watch work with my phone?
faq.a: Only with its own brand. The Apple Watch pairs properly with an iPhone and not with Android at all; the Samsung Galaxy Watch 6 and Google Pixel Watch 2 pair properly with Android. The budget trackers and the Citizen hybrid work with either. It is the most common expensive mistake in this category, so check which phone you have before choosing between the £59.95 and £64.95 rows.

That the call goes through your phone. The watch is acting as a speaker and microphone linked over Bluetooth, so if your phone is in another room the watch will not make the call. Only LTE models — like the Samsung Galaxy Watch 6 LTE at £54.95 — work with your phone left behind, and that needs a separate data plan from your network.

faq.q: How long does the battery last?
faq.a: It depends entirely on which type you buy, and this is the real dividing line. Budget trackers such as the £19.99 ZL02 run about a week. The Citizen hybrid runs about two weeks. Full smartwatches like the Galaxy Watch 6 and the Apple Watch SE run about a day or two, because they have a processor and a bright screen. No watch on this page gives you both.

faq.q: Are these pictures of the actual watches?
faq.a: No. Every picture in this department is a generated marketing graphic rather than a photograph of the unit, so none of them shows you the exact item that will arrive. That is a limitation of how the listings are made, not of the watches. What we have done instead is check every picture on this page against one question: does the graphic argue with the store? Does it print a price the store does not charge, or a rating, award or review count the store cannot back? Two wearables are left off for failing that — the Galaxy Watch SM-R840 and the Galaxy Watch 6 — which is why they are described and priced without a picture. Three of the pictures we do show carry a GPS icon, and those three watches do not have GPS. We would rather tell you that plainly than let the icon speak for itself.
